cleanIntro: This guide follows Beretta's manual for its over-and-under family, which never prints the 686 Silver Pigeon I name, so check your variant against it. A break-open comes apart into three pieces and back together in a minute, so the job is less about disassembly than about two surfaces: the bores, and the hinge pin area where the receiver and fore-end iron carry the load of every shot. Beretta is emphatic about the second one.

steps.title: Muzzle safe, safety on
steps.action: This guide follows Beretta's over-and-under family manual, which does not name the 686 Silver Pigeon I, so check your variant against it. Point the barrels in a safe direction and engage the safety before the top lever is touched.
steps.prose: Everything after this is done with the gun pointed somewhere a discharge would hurt nobody. The safety goes on first because the next move opens the gun with your hand near the trigger guard.
steps.quote: Aim the barrels in a safe direction and engage the safety
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — USE — UNLOADING, printed p.17

steps.title: Top lever right, barrels down, chambers emptied by hand
steps.action: Turn the top lever to the right and tilt the barrels down. Spent shells are thrown clear; unfired cartridges are only raised, so lift them out with your fingers and look into both chambers until you can see they are empty.
steps.prose: The extractors lift a live round just far enough to grip it. A cartridge left half-raised in one chamber is the classic miss on a two-barrel gun, so look at both.
steps.quote: When the shotgun is opened after shooting, the extractors will eject the spent shells and raise the unfired cartridges to make manual removal easier.
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — USE — UNLOADING, printed p.17

steps.title: Unloaded before anything comes apart
steps.action: Before the fore-end comes off, confirm once more that both chambers are empty. Beretta puts this demand at the head of the disassembly chapter, in capitals.
steps.prose: On a break-open this is the easiest check in shooting, and that is exactly why it gets skipped. It takes two seconds with the gun already open.
steps.quote: ALWAYS MAKE SURE THAT THE SHOTGUN IS UNLOADED BEFORE BEGINNING DISASSEMBLY PROCEDURES.
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — DISASSEMBLY, printed p.18

steps.title: Fore-end catch lever down
steps.action: Close the gun, then pull the fore-end catch lever down. It releases the fore-end iron from the barrel hook mechanism; nothing under it is spring-loaded against you.
steps.prose: The fore-end is what holds the barrels to the hinge pins once the gun is open, so it comes off first with the gun closed.
steps.quote: Pull the fore-end catch lever down
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — DISASSEMBLY, printed p.18

steps.title: Fore-end forward and off
steps.action: Turn the fore-end forward and take it off the receiver. It comes away as one piece with its iron.
steps.prose: Set it down iron-side up. The iron's bearing surfaces are one of the two areas Beretta singles out for oil, and they pick up grit from a bench.
steps.quote: Turn the fore-end forward to remove it from the receiver
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — DISASSEMBLY, printed p.18

steps.title: ⛔ Top lever right, and HOLD the barrels as they tip
steps.action: Turn the top lever to the right and tilt the barrels down, holding them firmly. Without the fore-end there is nothing to stop them sliding off the hinge pins and onto the floor.
steps.prose: This is the step where over-and-under barrels get dropped. Keep one hand under the barrels the whole time the lever is open.
steps.quote: Tilt the barrels downward, holding them firmly to stop them from sliding off the hinge pins completely and falling.
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — DISASSEMBLY, printed p.18

steps.title: Barrels up and out
steps.action: Lift the barrels gently upward and out of the receiver. The top lever stays open when they are out, and that is correct.
steps.prose: Do not force the lever closed on an empty receiver. Beretta's assembly instructions warn that closing it during assembly can damage the extractors, and the barrels go back in with it open.
steps.quote: Lift the barrels gently upward and out of the receiver
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — DISASSEMBLY, printed p.18

steps.title: Snap caps out, and never dry-fire without them
steps.action: If you put snap caps in to let the hammers down, take them out now. Tilting the barrels recocks the hammers, so if you want the springs at rest for storage, decock again on snap caps, never on empty chambers.
steps.prose: Dropping a hammer on an empty over-and-under hits the firing pin with nothing to stop it. Beretta's answer is snap caps, which let the gun be dry fired without damage.
steps.quote: It is equally important not to decock the hammers by pulling the trigger on an unloaded shotgun without snap-caps; the action could damage the firing pins.
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — USE — DECOCKING THE HAMMERS, printed p.17

steps.title: Clean at the end of every outing, chokes checked
steps.action: At the end of each day's shooting, clean the gun and check the chokes are properly tight. Where the metal has no protective surface treatment, clean and lubricate it after every use.
steps.prose: Beretta ties the choke check to the clean on purpose. A choke that works loose while you shoot is a bore obstruction in the making.
steps.quote: At the end of a hunting or shotting session, clean the shotgun and make sure the chokes are properly tightened.
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — MAINTENANCE, printed p.20

steps.title: ⛔ Rod in from the CHAMBER end, every time
steps.action: Put a cotton cloth soaked in gun cleaner on the rod, with a bronze brush if the residue needs it, and always enter at the cartridge chamber. Then run a clean dry cloth through to take the cleaner out, then a lightly oiled one.
steps.prose: Entering from the muzzle drags grit across the crown and the choke threads. The chamber end is the only way in.
steps.quote: Always insert the cleaning rod into the cartridge chamber
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — MAINTENANCE, printed p.20

steps.title: Inner face of the receiver, but keep oil OUT of the pin holes
steps.action: Clean the inner face of the receiver, especially around the firing pin holes, and oil it lightly. No oil goes into the firing pin holes themselves.
steps.prose: Oil in the pin holes thickens, slows the pins and gives light strikes in the cold. Lightly is the operative word here.
steps.quote: Do not allow oil to enter the firing pin holes
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — MAINTENANCE, printed p.20

steps.title: ⛔ The hinge pin area must never be dry
steps.action: Clean the hinge pin area and the fore-end iron and oil them lightly, every time. This is the coupling that takes the load of every shot.
steps.prose: Beretta is plain that if this area is not properly oiled, parts can seize or the gun can malfunction. It is the one surface on the gun that is never left dry.
steps.quote: The hinge pin area is a very important coupling area. The receiver and fore-end iron are subject to very high loads and if not properly oiled, could cause seizing of parts or shotgun malfunctioning.
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — MAINTENANCE, printed p.21

steps.title: Outside wiped down; gun and case dry before storage
steps.action: Wipe every outer surface free of dirt, sweat and fingerprints and put a thin film of good gun oil over it with a soft cloth. Then check that the gun and its case or slip are both perfectly dry before it goes away.
steps.prose: A damp case will rust a gun that was put away clean, which is why Beretta names the case and not only the gun.
steps.quote: Before storing the shotgun, always check the conditions of the shotgun and case, which must be perfectly dry.
steps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — MAINTENANCE, printed p.21

deepSteps.title: Butt plate off
deepSteps.action: Loosen the two butt-plate fastening screws and take the butt plate off. Grease the screws and the screwdriver tip first, because a butt plate is easy to mark.
deepSteps.prose: This is the only step past the field strip that Beretta's book gives an owner. The grease is the book's own advice, given as a caution.
deepSteps.quote: loosen the two fastening screws “A” and take off the butt plate “B”;
deepSteps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — STOCK REMOVAL, printed p.19

deepSteps.title: Stock bolt out, stock off
deepSteps.action: Put the Allen key into the stock bolt and unscrew it counter-clockwise until the stock comes away completely from the receiver. It goes back on in reverse order.
deepSteps.prose: If a guide bushing is fitted it steers the key onto the bolt head and helps the stock come away straight.
deepSteps.quote: unscrew the bolt counterclockwise until the stock comes away completely from the receiver.
deepSteps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — STOCK REMOVAL, printed p.19

deepSteps.title: ⛔ And that is the end of what Beretta publishes
deepSteps.action: Past the stock there is nothing in this book for an owner. No repairs without the experience or training for them, no alterations or adjustments to any part, original Beretta spare parts only. Anything the gun needs to function goes to the manufacturer or a qualified person.
deepSteps.prose: The book's trigger-group removal is reserved for replacement or extraordinary maintenance and its firing-pin replacement is a parts job; neither is carried here. This guide stops where Beretta stops.
deepSteps.quote: Any alteration or intervention necessary for the shotgun to function must be carried out by the manufacturer or by a qualified person.
deepSteps.cite: Beretta Over-and-Unders User Manual — UNKNOWN — read off the manual's own pages — MAINTENANCE, printed p.21

cleaning.name: BORES
tasks: Clean at the end of every outing and check the chokes are properly tight
Rod always in from the CHAMBER end, never the muzzle
Gun cleaner on a cotton cloth, bronze brush only if needed
Dry cloth through to remove cleaner residue, then a light oil
⛔ Never too much oil: excess oil or grease can obstruct the bore

cleaning.name: RECEIVER FACE
tasks: Inner face cleaned, especially round the firing pin holes
⛔ Oil lightly, and never INTO the firing pin holes

cleaning.name: HINGE PIN & FORE-END IRON
tasks: Hinge pin area cleaned and lubricated every time
Fore-end iron surfaces cleaned and oiled lightly

cleaning.name: OUTSIDE & STORAGE
tasks: Dirt, sweat and fingerprints off every outer surface
Thin film of good gun oil on a soft cloth
⛔ Never spray or apply oil to cartridges
⛔ Gun AND case perfectly dry before it is put away

reassembly: ⛔ Never put the barrels into the receiver with the fore-end fitted on them.
Top lever turned to the right, and left open: closing it during assembly can damage the extractors.
Barrels into the receiver so the receiver's hinge pins enter their slots in the barrels.
Tilt the barrels up slowly and gently, making sure the extractor lugs enter their slots in the receiver; the top lever snapping back to centre means they are locked.
Fore-end iron hooked onto the receiver, then the fore-end turned up and pressed firmly against the barrels to engage the barrel hook mechanism.
⛔ The fore-end is only locked when its lever is ALIGNED IN ITS SLOT. Check it.
fncheck: Reassembled and unloaded: the top lever has snapped back to centre, so the barrels are locked; the fore-end catch lever sits aligned in its slot, not merely close to it. Work the safety, then open and close the gun once more to confirm the barrels seat without force.
